title: Inspired, then calm
hookLine: when the mind is scattered, turn to an inspiring theme, then return

cards: Ananda goes one morning to a dwelling of nuns.

They sit with him and tell him their practice is going well: we dwell, they say, with our minds well established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and we notice a progress, one stage after another.
Ananda is glad, and later he reports it to the Buddha, who agrees: so it is. Then he adds a frank note about how meditation goes.
While someone is contemplating, a fever can arise, or sluggishness, or the mind can scatter outward. What then?

teach.b: Whether you're contemplating the body, or feelings, or mind, or phenomena, the Buddha says, if a fever arises, or sluggishness, or the mind scatters outward, direct the mind toward some inspiring sign, something that lifts the heart.

The Pali word, pasadaniya, means something that brings serene confidence. The sutta doesn't say what it is; it might be the Buddha, a teacher, a good deed you remember, a line you love. Then watch the sequence.
When the mind turns to the inspiring sign, gladness arises.
From gladness, joy. With a joyful mind, the body grows calm. With a calm body, one feels happiness.
Then the second half, the part that's easy to skip. Having been lifted, you withdraw: you set the inspiring image down and return to the original practice.
The person then knows, the text says: I'm not thinking and examining; I'm mindful within, and at ease. Not grit your teeth and force it. Not give up and scroll.
Lift the heart first, then come back. The Buddha calls this directed development, and he names undirected development too, for when the mind is already steady and doesn't need the detour.
The nuns' report was good news, and his answer still makes room for scattered days, with a way back that starts with gladness.

how: Some meditation teachers suggest recollecting the Buddha, a teacher or one's own good deeds when practice turns dull or restless, before returning to the main object such as the breath.

o: fired up to force the mind into stillness
struck by a sudden vision sent from the gods
lifted by something that brings joy and trust

games.q: inspired, then calm: tap the pairs.

s: the sutta says scattered minds come only to beginners
the nuns were practicing well, and the Buddha still speaks of fever, sluggishness and scattering.
after the inspiring sign, you set it down and return
the text describes withdrawing to the original practice.
the sequence runs gladness, joy, calm, happiness, concentration
each step leads to the next.

games.q: you're meditating well, and suddenly the mind scatters outward. what does the Buddha suggest?
o: turn to an inspiring sign, then return.
games.why: lift the heart first with something inspiring; gladness, joy and calm follow. then set it down and go back to the practice.

practice: Start with the breath, and if the mind is busy or dull, don't fight it: bring to mind one image that lifts you, a face you admire, a kind act you once saw, a sunrise, the Buddha's still figure, a line you love.
Stay with it until a little gladness rises and the body softens. Then set the image down gently and come back to the breath, with a lighter heart.

wordCard.voice: Inspired. When the mind scatters, the Buddha tells Ananda, turn it to an inspiring sign, let gladness and calm arise, then return to the practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pasadaniya: inspiring, bringing serene confidence; related to pasada, clarity or trust.

carryVoice: Your line: look for what lifts you. Gladness first, and then the way back. That's day six hundred seventy-four.
